newsitem.title: UK: Major cites Italy to warn Britons on voting reform.
newsitem.headline: Major cites Italy to warn Britons on voting reform.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major has seized on Italy's record of revolving-door governments to try to scare British voters away from electoral reform.

Major said the Italian experience -- 55 governments since the end of World War Two -- was a sobering reminder of the chaos that could result if Britain were to scrap its first-past-the- post voting system.

"This is a foolish policy to pursue. It is alien to the British tradition," Major said on Tuesday, referring to talks between the opposition Labour Party and the minority Liberal Democrats on a referendum.
"It (proportional representation) essentially means a minor party in a coalition can at any stage bring down that coalition government, and increasingly determine what the policy is."

He launched his attack at the first of a series of "presidential" news conferences which he plans to hold in a bid to close a 20-point Labour opinion poll lead in the run-up to a general election expected within four months
Critics said it was special pleading by the leader of a party which has won an overall majority at the last four British general elections while polling around 43 percent of the vote.

Major cited Labour and Liberal plans for constitutional reform, their alleged willingness to cede further powers to the European Union and Britain's booming economy as the three key electoral themes he will pursue.

Opinion polls suggest that most voters are ready to embrace electoral reform as part of an overhaul of Britain's 19th century constitution which tends to give almost unfettered power to a party that wins over half the seats in parliament.

But Major believes that deep down many people fear the unpredictable result of changing the present system, just as they worry that Labour plans for a tax-raising Scottish parliament could bring the break-up of Britain.
He has seized on talks which senior Labour and Liberal figures are currently holding to seek agreement on a programme of constitutional change for the next parliament.
The parties have already agreed on Scottish devolution and other issues such as a bill of rights.

Now the Liberals -- who won 20 seats in the 651-member House of Commons at the last election after polling over 17 percent of the vote -- are urging Labour leader Tony Blair to declare he will support voting reform in the planned referendum.
They argue such a change could put the centre-left in the driving seat of British politics since Labour and the Liberals between them consistently poll more than half the vote.

British constitutional reform advocates said Major's citing of Italy, which recently revised its electoral system, was misleading since most other West European states also use proportional voting to elect members of parliament.
